newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani industrialists seek bold budget moves.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani industrialists seek bold budget moves.

text.p: Pakistani businessmen are urging Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif to take politically tough decisions in Friday's 1997/98 (July-June) budget to stimulate industrial growth and resuscitate the ailing economy.
Sharif's 16-week-old government, with the muscle of a huge parliamentary majority, faces a tough task in underpinning Pakistan's shaky finances while simultaneously moving to break out of recession.
Pakistan aims to cut its budget deficit to five percent of gross domestic product in 1997/98 from 6.3 percent in 1996/97 and current account gap to five percent from seven percent.
This year's GDP growth is forecast at a meagre 3.1 percent against a 6.1 percent target, while the trade deficit is projected at $3.6 billion, just below last year's $3.7 billion.
Pakistan paid $3.9 billion in debt servicing in the first nine months of 1996/97 on its external debt of $29 billion.

"The government has no option but to revive the economy," Mian Latif, a leading textile industrialist, told Reuters. "There is no room to play around. If they (the government) do not deliver, they will not last. We are standing on sand."
Another prominent businessman, Tariq Saigol, said Sharif must cut spending, broaden the tax base to bring in agriculture, retail trade and services, and enforce fiscal discipline.
"Loss-making corporations have to be closed or restructured, the government has to be downsized, loans have to be recovered, unions have to be controlled," Saigol said.
"Banks have to be reformed and the cost of financial intermediation has to be brought down," he added.

Saigol, at the head of one of Pakistan's biggest industrial empires, said he had urged the government not to buckle under political compulsions. "Lip service won't make it happen. In practical terms, these unhappy decisions have to be taken and there is a real political cost," he said.

The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI) has proposed that the government amend the constitution to enable the federal government to levy farm income tax, hitherto a preserve of provincial governments.
"Now that the present government has a massive majority in parliament it must not shy away from its national responsibility and obligation to end the gross injustice," a FPCCI report said.
Only about one million of Pakistan's 138 million people pay direct taxes and most of its wealthiest agricultural landlords have paid little or no income tax in its 50-year history.
Saigol said the government must comply strictly with the public borrowing target of 58 billion rupees ($1.432 billion) set by the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP).

"It is an ambitious target, but the problems are so serious that unless we do set very ambitious and difficult targets, I don't think we will be able to make a breakthrough," he said. "A lot of belt tightening is required."
He said interest rates had to be reduced from the current 24 percent a year and government borrowing controlled so that it did not crowd out the cash-starved private sector.
Latif said the government had to give equal emphasis to agriculture and industry to ensure balanced growth.
"Our country and our industry is based on agriculture," he said. "If industry is neglected, agriculture won't survive and if agriculture is neglected, industry won't survive."
"The government's main task is to establish that balance and if both grow in parallel, Pakistan can get out of its economic crisis," Latif said.
